title: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
summary: How ACORN keeps HNSW search fast under arbitrary filters: predicate subgraph traversal, gamma-expanded lists, M_beta compression, ACORN-1, the pre-filter fallback, a lab, and how engines ship it.
outcomes: Explain why strict filtered search on a normal HNSW graph gets stuck and why HNSW pruning is unsafe for predicates
Compute expected passing neighbors per node and the chance a node becomes a dead end at a given selectivity
Trace ACORN-gamma's compression rule and the two-hop lookup that recovers pruned neighbors
Compare ACORN-gamma and ACORN-1 on build time, memory and search speed using the paper's numbers
Choose gamma from a minimum selectivity and decide when a query should fall back to pre-filtering
Implement ACORN-gamma and ACORN-1 lookups and measure recall@10, distances and predicate checks against filtered HNSW
Predict how Weaviate, Lucene/Elasticsearch and Qdrant route a filtered query and when their ACORN-1 variants run

lessons.title: Why a filter breaks greedy search on an HNSW graph

blocks.md: A **hybrid query** asks for the $K$ nearest vectors that also satisfy a structured predicate, such as `category = shoes AND price < 50`. The **selectivity** $s$ of the predicate is the fraction of records that pass it. The ACORN paper (Patel, Kraft, Guestrin, Zaharia, SIGMOD 2024) names three ways to answer such queries and argues all three fall short. The name stands for ANN Constraint-Optimized Retrieval Network, where the constraints are the query's predicates.

From the previous course: **pre-filtering** finds every passing record and brute-forces them, costing $O(sn)$ distance computations, which is exact but linear in $sn$. **Post-filtering** searches the unfiltered HNSW index and drops failing results, so it must over-fetch about $K/s$ candidates, and it degrades badly when passing vectors sit far from the query. **Specialized indices** such as Filtered-DiskANN and NHQ build the filter into the graph, but only for small sets of equality filters known in advance. Filtered-DiskANN builds on Vamana, the graph-construction algorithm behind DiskANN, and comes in two forms: FilteredVamana, one graph whose pruning looks at labels, and StitchedVamana, one graph per label overlaid into a single index. The method called native hybrid queries (NHQ) builds one composite graph whose edges are chosen using vectors and attributes together.

Besides selectivity and dataset size, the paper studies a third workload property that hurts post-filtering: **query correlation**. If the passing points cluster near the query (positive correlation), post-filtering finds them quickly. If they cluster far away (negative correlation), the unfiltered search walks toward the wrong region, and the paper notes the worst case is $O(n)$.

Now the obvious fix: during graph search, just ignore neighbors that fail the predicate and only walk among passing nodes. This is **predicate subgraph traversal**: searching the subgraph induced by the passing points $X_p$, the subset of the dataset $X$ that satisfies predicate $p$, keeping only edges that join two passing points. It only computes distances for passing nodes, so it never wastes work on failures. The figure shows what happens when you try it on an ordinary graph.

blocks.title: Strict filtered search on a plain graph gets stuck

scenes.caption: Ten points on a grid, each linked to its 2 nearest points (M = 2, ties broken alphabetically). Green nodes pass the filter (5 of 10, so s = 0.5). Badges are distances to the query for passing nodes. The true filtered answer is B at 3.16.
Search starts at the entry point I (7.81). Strict filtering means we only step onto, and only compute distances for, nodes that pass. I has one passing neighbor: H.
At H (5.83) the neighbors are A, G and I. A and G fail the filter, and I is farther than H. Greedy search stops and returns H, missing B, D and J entirely.
Why: this is the predicate subgraph, only passing nodes and edges between them. It splits into three pieces, {I, H}, {D, B} and {J} alone. J has zero passing neighbors.

The real route to B runs H, G, J, E, D, B. G and E fail the filter, so strict traversal cannot use them. The overall nearest point, E (2.24), also fails, which is why post-filtering would waste work here.

blocks.prompt: In the plain graph ($M = 2$) each node has 2 or 3 links and $s = 0.5$. Suppose a node's neighbors pass independently with probability $s$. What is the chance that a node with exactly 2 neighbors has no passing neighbor at all?
blocks.reveal: $(1-s)^2 = 0.5^2 = 0.25$. One node in four is a dead end, which is exactly what happened to J. With degree $d$ the chance is $(1-s)^d$, so the fix is to make $d$ large enough that $(1-s)^d$ is tiny. That is the core of ACORN-$\gamma$, where gamma is the factor by which ACORN multiplies the length of every node's neighbor list.

blocks.md: HNSW's construction makes this worse. Its neighbor heuristic prunes the edge $v$ to $b$ whenever some kept neighbor $a$ is closer to $b$ than $v$ is, expecting search to reach $b$ through $a$. That pruning is **metadata-blind**: if $v$ and $b$ pass the predicate but $a$ fails, the detour no longer exists in the predicate subgraph, and the edge was pruned for nothing.

The paper frames the goal with an **oracle partition index**: if you knew the predicate at build time, you would build a separate HNSW over just $X_p$ and search it in about $O(\log(sn) + K)$. That beats both pre- and post-filtering at every selectivity and correlation, but one index per possible predicate is impossible when predicates are regexes, date ranges, or keyword lists. ACORN's aim is to make *any* predicate subgraph of one shared index behave like that oracle HNSW.

Predicate subgraph traversal is the right search strategy (no distance computations wasted on failing nodes), but on a normal HNSW graph the predicate subgraph is sparse and disconnected. ACORN changes how the graph is built, or how neighbors are looked up, so that the predicate subgraph stays connected for any predicate.

blocks.question: In the figure, strict filtered search returns H. Which change to the search alone (same graph) would reliably find B?
options: Increase ef so the candidate list holds more passing nodes
Start from a different fixed entry point chosen at build time
Step through failing nodes such as G and E with a beam of ef 2 or more, at the cost of computing their distances
Truncate each neighbor list to M before filtering
blocks.explain: From I the only reachable passing nodes are I and H, so a bigger ef cannot help: there is nothing else in the predicate subgraph component to add. Walking through failing nodes reaches B but spends distance computations on non-results, which is the in-traversal filtering cost ACORN wants to avoid. A fixed entry point does not know the predicate.

blocks.question: A workload filters images by label 'cat' while queries are photos of dogs, so passing points sit far from each query. Which baseline suffers most?
options: Pre-filtering, because selectivity drops
Post-filtering, because the unfiltered search heads toward the wrong region
Neither, since both are exact
The oracle partition index
blocks.explain: This is negative query correlation. Post-filtering's unfiltered search converges near dog photos that fail the filter, and it must expand very far to collect K cats. Pre-filtering's cost depends only on how many records pass, not on where they sit.

lessons.title: ACORN-gamma: expand every neighbor list by gamma

blocks.md: ACORN-$\gamma$ makes two changes to HNSW construction. First, **neighbor list expansion**: where HNSW collects $M$ candidate edges per node, ACORN-$\gamma$ collects $M \cdot \gamma$ approximate nearest neighbors, found with an ordinary (metadata-agnostic) search over the graph built so far. Second, it **drops HNSW's RNG-style pruning** on those lists, because that pruning is metadata-blind. RNG stands for relative neighborhood graph: it keeps the edge between $u$ and $v$ only if no third point $w$ is closer to both $u$ and $v$ than they are to each other. HNSW's neighbor heuristic applies a local version of that test to each node's candidates, which is the pruning from lesson 1. A kNN graph has no such test: it simply links each node to its k nearest points. So each level approximates a kNN graph rather than a relative neighborhood graph.

The search changes in one place: the neighbor lookup. At each visited node $v$ on level $l$, ACORN scans $N^l(v)$, keeps only neighbors that pass the predicate, giving the filtered list $N^l_p(v)$, and **truncates it to the first $M$**. The raised $l$ on $N$ is a level label, not an exponent: it names the list stored for $v$ on level $l$, and the subscript $p$ marks the part of that list that passes predicate $p$. Everything else is HNSW's greedy beam search with candidate list size ef. The truncation keeps the per-node cost bounded by $M$ distance computations, even though the stored list is $\gamma$ times longer. (The reference code allows $2M$ on level 0, HNSW's bottom-level degree; lesson 5 follows it.)
Why $\gamma$? If a node's $M\gamma$ neighbors pass independently with probability $s$ (no predicate clustering, which the paper treats as the worst case), the number that pass is binomial with mean:

blocks.tex: \mathbb{E}\,|N^l_p(v)| = |N^l(v)| \cdot s = \gamma M s \;\geq\; M \quad\text{whenever}\quad s \geq s_{\min} = \frac{1}{\gamma}
blocks.caption: In words: expected passing neighbors = list length (gamma times M) times s. Choose gamma = 1/s_min, the lowest selectivity the graph should serve. Then for any s at least s_min, gamma M s is at least gamma M s_min = M, so the predicate subgraph's expected degree is at least M.

blocks.md: The figure uses the paper's settings for two of its benchmark datasets. **SIFT1M** is one million 128-dimensional SIFT descriptors (scale-invariant feature transform, a classic hand-crafted image feature); the paper gives each vector a random label from 1 to 12, so an equality filter on one label passes 1 in 12 records. **LAION** is a set of 512-dimensional CLIP embeddings of web images (CLIP is a model that maps images and text into one vector space), and its filters test each image's caption and keyword list.

blocks.title: Expected passing neighbors per node vs selectivity

curves.label: ACORN list (gamma x M x s)

scenes.caption: M = 32, gamma = 12 (the paper's SIFT1M setting). At s = 1/12 an ACORN list of 384 expects 32 passing neighbors, exactly M, while HNSW's 64-slot bottom list expects only 5.33.
gamma = 30 (the LAION setting) moves s_min down to 1/30 = 0.033. Below s_min even the expanded list expects fewer than M passing neighbors, which is where ACORN hands the query to pre-filtering.
gamma = 1 is plain HNSW density: the green line drops onto M x s and the predicate subgraph only has degree M when nearly everything passes.

blocks.md: The expected value is not the whole story: the chance that a node gets **zero** passing neighbors, and so becomes a dead end like J, is $(1-s)^{M\gamma}$. With $M = 32$ and $s = 1/12$, HNSW's upper-level list of $M = 32$ has a 6.2% chance of being empty and its bottom list of 64 a 0.38% chance. ACORN-$\gamma$ with $\gamma = 12$ has 384 slots: $(11/12)^{384} \approx 3.1 \times 10^{-15}$. The paper bounds the probability that any node on the search path disconnects by $O(\log n \cdot (1-s)^{M\gamma})$, which decays exponentially in $\gamma$.

blocks.title: ACORN-gamma: denser lists keep the subgraph connected

scenes.caption: Same points, now built with gamma = 2: each node keeps its M x gamma = 4 nearest points instead of 2 (21 edges instead of 12). Simplified: one layer, kNN links, no HNSW levels.
The predicate subgraph now has edges H to J and J to D, so the five passing nodes form one chain: I, H, J, D, B. Expected passing neighbors per node: M x gamma x s = 4 x 0.5 = 2 = M.
Search from I (7.81). Its list is A, C, G, H. Filter it to passing nodes, keep at most M = 2: only H. Move to H (5.83). No distance is computed for A, C or G.
At H the list is A, G, I, J. Passing: I and J. J (4.12) is closer than H, so move to J.
At J the list is D, E, G, H. Passing: D and H. D (3.61) is closer, move to D.
At D the passing neighbors are B and J. B (3.16) is closer. At B the only passing neighbor is D (3.61), farther, so search stops and returns B, the true filtered nearest neighbor.

blocks.md:
**Getting into the subgraph.** ACORN keeps HNSW's single fixed entry point, which may fail the predicate. Search runs in two stages. In stage 1 it filters each upper level's neighbor list and drops a level whenever the filtered list is empty. Because the expansion makes upper levels dense, any level with fewer than $M\gamma$ nodes is fully connected (each node's list has room for every other node on that level), so as soon as a level holds one passing node, the search reaches it in one hop. Stage 2 is then greedy search over the predicate subgraph: beam 1 on the remaining upper levels, beam ef on level 0.

The reference code runs the upper levels with one greedy rule: move to the closest passing neighbor in the filtered list if it is closer than the current node, or whatever its distance while the current node fails; when no move is left, drop a level and keep the node. The lab in lesson 5 uses the same rule.

blocks.title: Stage 1: from the fixed entry point into the predicate subgraph

scenes.caption: Simplified toy: M = 2, gamma = 3, so a list holds up to 6 entries. Level 2 has 2 nodes and level 1 has 5, so every node links to every other node on its level. Only F passes (s = 0.2).

Stage 1 starts at the fixed entry A on level 2. Its filtered list is empty (B fails), so search stays on A and drops a level. A level of L nodes is empty of passing nodes with probability (1 - s)^L: 0.8^2 = 0.64 here.
On level 1, A's list holds all 4 other nodes. Filtering it leaves only F, so one hop reaches the predicate subgraph. A distance is computed for F alone.

F passes, so it is the entry for level 0, where stage 2 runs the beam search over passing nodes. Had level 1 held no passing node either (0.8^5 = 0.33), search would drop again and start level 0 from A.

blocks.tex: P(\text{no passing node on a level of } L \text{ nodes}) = (1-s)^{L}
blocks.caption: Each node passes independently with probability s (no predicate clustering), so all L fail with probability (1 - s) multiplied L times.

blocks.md: How often does stage 1 have to drop a level? The lab in lesson 5 uses 100,000 SIFT vectors with $M = 32$; its upper levels hold 5, 88 and 3,086 nodes. At $s = 1/12$ the top level has no passing node with probability $(11/12)^5 = 0.65$, the 88-node level with $(11/12)^{88} = 0.00047$, and the 3,086-node level essentially never ($10^{-117}$). The 88-node level is also fully connected, since 87 other nodes fit in a list of $M\gamma = 384$. So the descent often finds nothing on the top level but almost always reaches a passing node in one hop on the next one.

The paper's analysis gives an expected search cost of $O((d+\gamma)\log(sn) + \log(1/s))$ for vector dimension $d$, close to the oracle partition's $O(d \log(sn))$. The $\log(1/s)$ term is stage 1: the full index has about $\log n$ levels, while the $sn$ passing nodes, sampled at the same level rates, form a hierarchy of only about $\log(sn)$ levels, so the descent first crosses about $\log n - \log(sn) = \log(1/s)$ levels that are unlikely to hold a passing node. The $\gamma$ term is the cheap predicate check over up to $M\gamma$ stored neighbors per visited node; distances are still computed for at most $M$.

Misconception: "just raise M in HNSW". The paper notes that Qdrant's earlier densification idea did this, but $M$ also sets HNSW's level multiplier $m_L = 1/\ln M$, so raising it flattens the hierarchy, and HNSW is sensitive to its number of levels. ACORN keeps $M$ (and therefore $m_L$ and the level structure) fixed and expands the lists by $\gamma$ instead.

blocks.question: An index is built with M = 32 and gamma = 12 and searched with the paper's Algorithm 2. A query arrives with predicate selectivity s = 0.25. Roughly how many neighbors will the search compute distances for at a typical visited node?
options: 384, the whole stored list
96, all passing neighbors
At most 32: the passing neighbors are truncated to M
blocks.explain: About 384 x 0.25 = 96 neighbors pass, but ACORN truncates the filtered list to the first M = 32 before computing distances. The predicate is evaluated on up to 384 entries (cheap), distances on at most 32 (expensive). 8 would be plain HNSW's expectation.

blocks.question: Why does ACORN-gamma skip HNSW's RNG-based pruning when building neighbor lists?
options: It makes construction too slow
The pruned detour through a third node may fail the predicate, so the shortcut it relied on vanishes in the predicate subgraph
RNG pruning only works for cosine distance
HNSW never prunes at the bottom level
blocks.explain: HNSW drops edge v to b if some kept neighbor a is closer to b, trusting search to go v, a, b. For a predicate where v and b pass but a fails, that path does not exist. Without knowing predicates at build time you cannot prune safely, so ACORN keeps the near neighbors and uses a predicate-agnostic compression instead.

lessons.title: Paying for density: M_beta compression and two-hop recovery

blocks.md: Expanding every list by $\gamma$ costs memory and build time. HNSW-style indexes live in RAM, so a $\gamma = 12$ index that stored 384 neighbors per node on the bottom level would be several times larger than HNSW. ACORN-$\gamma$ attacks this where it matters most: the **bottom level**, which holds every node. Upper levels are small because a node reaches level $l$ with probability $M^{-l}$.

The idea is to store each node's nearby neighbors exactly and approximate the farther ones through two-hop lookups. A tunable parameter $M_\beta$ (between 0 and $M\gamma$) sets how many of the closest candidates are kept unconditionally. For the remaining candidates, in distance order, ACORN keeps a set $H$ of the chosen nodes' neighbors and applies one rule:

1. If candidate $c$ is already in $H$, prune it (some kept neighbor already links to it).
2. Otherwise keep $c$ and add all of $c$'s neighbors to $H$.
3. Stop when the candidates run out or when $|H|$ plus the number of chosen edges exceeds $M\gamma$.

$H$ is thrown away after construction. Nothing in this rule looks at metadata, so it is **predicate-agnostic**.

scenes.caption: Node v's candidate edges, nearest first. M = 3, gamma = 2, so there are M x gamma = 6 candidates. M_beta = 2. Known neighbor lists: c links to d, x, y; e links to f, z.
The first M_beta = 2 candidates, a and b, are kept unconditionally. These are the closest neighbors and are stored exactly.
c is not in H, so keep it and add its neighbors d, x, y to H. Chosen edges + |H| = 3 + 3 = 6, which does not exceed M x gamma = 6, so continue.
d is already in H (it is a neighbor of kept node c), so the edge v to d is pruned. Search can still find d two hops away, through c.
e is not in H: keep it and add f, z. Now 4 chosen + |H| = 5 gives 9, which exceeds 6, so pruning stops. f is never stored, but it is in H, reachable through e.
Stored list: a, b, c, e (4 slots, not 6). At search time, entries past position M_beta (c and e) are expanded to their own lists, so for a predicate passing b, d and f the lookup recovers b, d, f.

blocks.md:
**Search-time recovery.** The compression-aware lookup at node $v$ has two phases. For the first $M_\beta$ entries of $N^l(v)$ it just filters, as before. For entries past position $M_\beta$, it also expands each one into its own neighbor list (neighbors of neighbors) and filters those.

Why no pruned neighbor is lost: a candidate is pruned only if it is already in $H$, and $H$ receives only the neighbors of candidates kept *after* position $M_\beta$. The neighbors of the first $M_\beta$ entries are never added to $H$. So any node $x$ pruned from $v$'s list sits in the list of some kept neighbor $y$ that is itself stored beyond position $M_\beta$ of $v$'s list, exactly the entries the lookup expands, and the expansion finds $x$ whatever the predicate is.

blocks.title: Neighbor storage per node, SIFT1M settings

scenes.caption: Bottom-level slots per node. HNSW stores 2M = 64. ACORN-gamma with gamma = 12 would store M x gamma = 384. With compression the paper measures an average of 87.5 on SIFT1M (Table 6).

Bytes per node with 4-byte ids, counting average edges. Upper levels add 32/31 = 1.03 slots (HNSW) and 384/31 = 12.4 (ACORN). Totals: 260, 1586, 400. The reference code reserves M_beta + 1.5M = 112 level-0 slots, so real size is larger.

blocks.md: In the paper's measurements this keeps the overhead modest. Table 5 reports ACORN-$\gamma$ index sizes at most about 1.3x HNSW (SIFT1M: 0.98 GB vs 0.75 GB including vectors). Build time is the bigger cost: the paper's construction complexity is $O(n\gamma\log n\log\gamma)$ versus HNSW's $O(n \log n)$, and Table 4 shows SIFT1M taking 148.9 s vs 11.3 s for HNSW. Figure 12 shows search quality is fairly insensitive to $M_\beta$, so the paper uses $M_\beta = M$ or $2M$, while plain HNSW pruning on the same lists badly hurts hybrid search.

Upper levels stay uncompressed with up to $M\gamma$ neighbors (the paper's Table 6 shows level 1 at exactly 384 = $M\gamma$ on SIFT1M). That density is what makes small upper levels fully connected, which is how stage 1 of search finds a passing node quickly.

blocks.prompt: With M = 32, what fraction of nodes appear on level 1 or higher in an HNSW-style level assignment, and so would pay for an uncompressed 384-slot upper list?
blocks.reveal: A node's top level is $\lfloor -\ln(u)\, m_L \rfloor$ with $u$ drawn uniformly between 0 and 1 and $m_L = 1/\ln M$, so $P(\text{level} \geq 1) = e^{-1/m_L} = 1/M = 1/32$, about 3.1 percent. Expected upper-level slots per node are $M\gamma \sum_{l \geq 1} M^{-l} = 384/31 \approx 12.4$. That is why compressing only level 0 captures most of the savings.

blocks.question: During compression, candidate d is pruned from v's list because it is in H. At search time, under a predicate where d passes but kept neighbor c (which links to d) fails, can the search still reach d from v?
options: No, because c fails the predicate and is skipped
Yes, if c sits beyond position M_beta, because the lookup expands c's list before filtering
Only if d is within the first M_beta entries
Only with ACORN-1
blocks.explain: The two-hop expansion reads c's neighbor list regardless of whether c passes; the predicate is applied to the expanded entries. By construction, any pruned node was in H only because some later kept neighbor links to it, and entries past M_beta are exactly the ones the lookup expands.

blocks.question: You double M_beta from 32 to 64 on LAION. What is the main effect?
options: Bottom-level lists get longer and the index larger, with little change in search quality according to the paper
The minimum supported selectivity halves
Upper levels become compressed
Search switches from ACORN-gamma to ACORN-1
blocks.explain: M_beta is the number of nearest candidates stored without pruning on the compressed level, so raising it grows the bottom-level lists. The paper finds search fairly insensitive to M_beta (Figure 12). s_min is set by gamma, not M_beta.

lessons.title: ACORN-1: expand at search time instead of build time

blocks.md: ACORN-$\gamma$ pays at build time. **ACORN-1** moves the expansion to search time. Its index is ACORN-$\gamma$'s construction with $\gamma = 1$ and $M_\beta = M$, which the paper describes as the original HNSW index without pruning. At each visited node, the lookup gathers **all one-hop and two-hop neighbors**, applies the predicate, and truncates to $M$.

Intuition: a node with $M$ neighbors has up to about $M^2$ two-hop neighbors, so the expanded neighborhood plays the role of ACORN-$\gamma$'s long list. The cost is that the expanded set is a less precise stand-in for a node's true $M\gamma$ nearest neighbors, and the lookup reads more lists per visited node.

blocks.title: ACORN-1 neighbor lookup at node H

scenes.caption: Lookup at H with M = 2. H's stored list, nearest first, is G, A, I (plain graph from the figure).
First hop u = G. G itself fails the predicate, so it is not added, but its list is still scanned.
G's list: H is skipped (it is v), J passes and is added. This is the two-hop edge that reconnects H to J.
Next u = A, which fails. A's list contains I, which passes, so I is added.
u = I passes but is already in out, and I's list (A, H) adds nothing new. Truncate to M = 2 and return.

blocks.title: ACORN-1: two-hop lookups on the plain graph

scenes.caption: Back to the plain M = 2 graph (an HNSW-like build with no extra edges). ACORN-1 does not change the index; it changes the lookup: one-hop and two-hop neighbors, then filter, then keep M.
At H, neighbor G fails, but G's own list contains J, which passes. The lookup returns J and I. J (4.12) is closer than H (5.83), so move to J.
At J, both neighbors E and G fail. E's list holds D, G's list holds H. The lookup returns D and H. D (3.61) is closer, move to D.
At D, B passes directly (3.16). At B, the lookup finds only D. Search returns B, the true answer, with the same path as ACORN-gamma: I, H, J, D, B.

blocks.md:
**The tradeoff in numbers** (from the paper):

- Search: ACORN-1 reaches about 1.5x to 5x lower QPS (queries per second, the throughput measure) than ACORN-$\gamma$ at the same recall. Table 3 counts distance computations to reach Recall@10 = 0.8 on SIFT1M (on average 8 of the true 10 nearest passing vectors returned): 611 for ACORN-$\gamma$ vs 999.6 for ACORN-1.
- Build: ACORN-1 builds 9x to 53x faster than ACORN-$\gamma$ (SIFT1M 8.6 s vs 148.9 s; LAION-25M 705.3 s vs 38,007.5 s). In Table 4 it has the lowest build time of all methods, below the HNSW baseline.

The reference code (a fork of FAISS, Meta's open-source vector search library, class `IndexACORNFlat`, whose constructor takes `d, M, gamma`, a per-vector `metadata` list and `M_beta`) implements both variants in the same bottom-level lookup loop: when `gamma == 1` it expands every neighbor, otherwise it expands only entries past `M_beta`. Its README example builds ACORN-$\gamma$ with $\gamma = 12$, $M_\beta = 32$ and ACORN-1 with $\gamma = 1$, $M_\beta = 2M$ (the paper fixes $M_\beta = M$ for ACORN-1).

ACORN-$\gamma$ and ACORN-1 run the same search strategy, predicate subgraph traversal. They differ only in *where* the denser neighborhood comes from: stored at build time (ACORN-$\gamma$, faster search, slower build) or reconstructed from two-hop lookups at query time (ACORN-1, cheap build, somewhat slower search).

blocks.question: A team has an existing HNSW index over 500M vectors and cannot afford a long rebuild. Which approach fits best?
options: ACORN-gamma with gamma = 1/s_min
ACORN-1 style two-hop lookups over a standard HNSW-like graph
StitchedVamana with one graph per label
Raise M in the existing HNSW and rebuild
blocks.explain: ACORN-1 needs no expanded lists at build time; it reconstructs a denser neighborhood during search. Weaviate took this route: its blog says it kept vanilla HNSW indexing so existing data does not need re-indexing. ACORN-gamma and StitchedVamana both require heavier construction, and raising M flattens the hierarchy.

blocks.question: In the codetrace, why is J returned even though J is not in H's stored list?
options: J is H's entry point on the level
J was recovered from H's compressed M_beta entries
Truncation to M adds the next closest node
The lookup reads failing neighbor G's list and J passes the predicate
blocks.explain: ACORN-1 expands every neighbor u of H, including ones that fail, into u's own list, then filters. G fails but links to J, so J appears. There is no M_beta compression in ACORN-1 (it is fixed at M_beta = M).

lessons.title: Lab: build ACORN and measure it against filtered HNSW

blocks.md:
Time to test the central claim yourself: on a graph whose predicate subgraph stays connected, search computes distances only for passing nodes and still finds the true filtered neighbors. The lab uses **SIFT1M** from lesson 2, but only its first 100,000 vectors (128 dimensions) and its first 100 query vectors. As in the paper, every vector gets a random label from 1 to 12 and every query asks for one label, so $s = 1/12$. Ground truth is pre-filtering: brute force over the passing vectors, 8,334 distances per query on average.

Every number in this lesson comes from running the lab in one Python process (NumPy, two threads) on an Apple Silicon Mac. It counts **distance computations** and **predicate checks** rather than time, because Python overhead would swamp the comparison a C++ engine makes.

All methods share one HNSW-style level assignment ($M = 32$; levels of 100,000, 3,086, 88 and 5 nodes) and one fixed entry point:

- **Strict filtered HNSW**: an HNSW graph with the usual neighbor pruning (16.4 links per node on level 0), searched over passing nodes only.
- **Traverse-through**: the same graph, walking through failing nodes but returning only passing ones, which is how hnswlib's filter works.
- **ACORN-$\gamma$**, $\gamma = 12$: each list holds the $M\gamma = 384$ nearest nodes on its level, uncompressed.
- **ACORN-1**: lists of the $2M = 64$ nearest nodes on level 0 ($M$ above), no pruning, searched with the two-hop lookup.
- **ACORN-1 on the pruned graph**: the same two-hop lookup over the strict method's HNSW graph.

Simplification: the lists come from exact nearest neighbors computed offline, not from the insert-by-search build a real index uses.

blocks.caption: The two lookups from the lab. The paper's Algorithm 2 keeps M passing neighbors; the reference code stops at 2M on level 0, HNSW's bottom-level degree, and the lab follows the code: keep = 64 on level 0, 32 above.

Level-0 beam search (the paper's Algorithm 2) with distance counting. Upper levels: greedy descent (ef = 1, lesson 2's rule) with each method's own lookup; ACORN-1 uses the two-hop lookup over 32-entry lists. This function then rescores the entry node, so subtract 1 from the total count.

blocks.prompt: Strict filtered HNSW only steps onto passing nodes of a normal pruned HNSW graph. At s = 1/12, what recall@10 do you expect as ef grows from 10 to 160?
blocks.reveal: Almost none: 0.008 at ef = 10 and 0.107 at ef = 160, with only 20 to 170 distances computed. A node has about 16.4 links, so it expects $16.4/12 \approx 1.4$ passing neighbors. The walk is trapped in a small fragment of the predicate subgraph, and a bigger ef has nothing more to add. Lesson 1 drew the same failure on ten points.

blocks.title: Five methods on 100k SIFT vectors at s = 1/12

scenes.caption: Recall@10 in percent at ef = 40, from the lab run: 3.7, 100, 92.1, 96.7 and 96.0. Every method except strict traversal finds nearly all true filtered neighbors.
Distance computations per query at the same ef = 40: 57, 3,877, 712, 591 and 481. Traverse-through pays for every failing node it walks through.

Distances at the cheapest measured ef with recall@10 of at least 0.9: strict never gets there (0 shown), traverse-through 1,311 (ef 10), ACORN-1 712 (ef 40), ACORN-1 on HNSW 395 and ACORN-gamma 349 (ef 20). Pre-filtering needs 8,334.

blocks.md:
Reading the run:

- Strict traversal is cheap and useless, exactly as predicted.
- Traverse-through is accurate but already spends 1,311 distances at ef = 10. With random labels about 11 of every 12 of them go to nodes that can never be returned.
- ACORN-$\gamma$ reaches 0.926 recall with 349 distances and 0.986 with 994, against 8,334 for pre-filtering.
- ACORN-1 on its unpruned graph needs about twice ACORN-$\gamma$'s distances for 0.9, the same direction as the paper's Table 3 (999.6 vs 611 for 0.8 on SIFT1M).
- ACORN-1 over the *pruned* graph matched ACORN-$\gamma$ here (0.925 at 395, 0.994 at 902). A likely reason: pruning spreads a node's links in different directions, so their two-hop neighborhoods cover more ground than a plain nearest-neighbor list. Engines ship this variant (lesson 7).

blocks.title: ACORN-1 at s = 1/12: predicate checks vs distances

scenes.caption: Distance computations per query: 378, 516, 712, 998, 1,369. They grow with ef, but only passing nodes are ever scored.
Predicate checks per query: 9,452 to 119,092. Every two-hop lookup reads up to 64 lists of 64 entries and tests each id against the filter.
Checks per distance: 25, 32, 43, 60 and 87. Traverse-through, counting every list entry it reads, makes 1.6 to 3.4 (2.3 at ef 40). ACORN trades many cheap checks for few expensive distances.

blocks.md: Now drop to $s = 1/50$ (random labels 1 to 50) on the same $\gamma = 12$ index, so $s$ is below $s_{\min} = 1/12$. A 384-entry list now expects only $384/50 \approx 7.7$ passing neighbors, well under $M$. ACORN-$\gamma$'s recall falls to 0.448 at ef = 10 and only 0.760 at ef = 160. Strict HNSW returns nothing: the entry region has no passing neighbors at all. Traverse-through stays accurate but costs 4,134 to 24,533 distances, more than the 1,998 a pre-filter scan needs. At $s = 1/12$ it was still cheaper than pre-filtering (1,311 vs 8,334 at ef = 10), so in this run the crossover sits between 0.02 and 0.083, below the previous course's 0.15 on 10,000 vectors, as its cost model predicts for larger $n$. Rebuilding with $\gamma = 50$ (lists of 1,600, so $s_{\min} = 1/50$) restores the graph: 0.909 at ef = 10 and 0.990 at ef = 40 with 360 distances.

blocks.title: Below s_min: s = 1/50 on 100k SIFT vectors

scenes.caption: Recall@10 in percent at ef = 40: 63.3, 99.0, 74.9, 64.9 and 100. The gamma = 12 graph is used below its s_min and loses a third of the neighbors.
Distances per query at ef = 40: 158, 360, 336, 187 and 10,526. Traverse-through is exact but costs five times a pre-filter scan (1,998).
Recall at ef = 160: 76.0, 100, 86.1, 79.5 and 100. Raising ef helps the under-dense graphs slowly; gamma = 50 was already at 99 percent with ef = 40.

blocks.md:
Last, a **negatively correlated** workload: labels follow 12 k-means clusters of the vectors, and each query asks for one of the six clusters farthest from it (mean $s = 0.094$). Traverse-through now walks across the dataset, computing 44,000 to 55,500 distances per query, 44 to 56 percent of all vectors: the $O(n)$ worst case from lesson 1. ACORN-1 on the pruned graph needed 1,504 distances for 0.867 recall and 3,538 for 0.983; ACORN-$\gamma$ reached 0.862 at 3,067. Pre-filtering costs 9,349, exact.

Clustering also breaks the independence assumption behind $\gamma$. Inside the target cluster nearly every stored neighbor passes, so ACORN-$\gamma$'s lookup keeps just the nearest 64 of 384, a plain nearest-neighbor list; that probably explains why it trailed here.

In ACORN, predicate checks and distance computations come apart. In the run ACORN-1 made 25 to 87 predicate checks per distance; traverse-through, counting every list entry it read, made 1.6 to 3.4 (hnswlib itself calls its filter less often than it computes distances). A check can be one bit in a bitset; a distance reads a 512-byte vector and does 128 multiply-adds. Trading many checks for few distances is the whole method, and it only pays while the graph stays dense enough (s at least s_min).

blocks.question: In the lab run, ACORN-gamma built with gamma = 12 gives 0.96 recall@10 at s = 1/12 but only 0.63 at s = 1/50 (ef = 40). Which two knobs fix the s = 1/50 queries?
options: Raise M to 64 at build time, since more links per node can replace gamma
Raise ef to 1,000 on the same index; ef alone recovers the missing neighbors
Switch those queries to traverse-through, which is exact and cheaper than pre-filtering
Rebuild with gamma = 50 so s_min = 1/50, or send queries estimated below 1/12 to pre-filtering
blocks.explain: s = 1/50 is below s_min = 1/12, so a 384-entry list expects 7.7 passing neighbors. gamma = 50 gave 0.990 at 360 distances; pre-filtering is exact at 1,998. ef helps slowly (0.760 at ef 160). Traverse-through needed 10,526 distances at ef = 40, about 5x a pre-filter scan. Raising M also flattens the hierarchy (lesson 2).

blocks.question: Traverse-through and ACORN-1 both read failing nodes' neighbor lists. What does ACORN-1 avoid that traverse-through pays for?
options: Distance computations for failing nodes: it only checks the predicate on the ids it finds
Predicate checks: ACORN-1 evaluates fewer predicates per query
Reading the graph: ACORN-1 never touches a failing node
The descent: ACORN-1 starts at a passing node chosen at build time
blocks.explain: In the lab run at s = 1/12 and ef = 40, ACORN-1 made 30,653 predicate checks but only 712 distances; traverse-through made 8,756 checks and 3,877 distances. ACORN-1 does more checks, not fewer, and it reads failing nodes' lists to find two-hop neighbors. Both start from the same fixed entry point.

lessons.title: Choosing gamma, falling back to pre-filter, and real results

blocks.md: **Setting $\gamma$.** The paper's simple rule is $\gamma = 1/s_{\min}$, where $s_{\min}$ is the lowest selectivity the graph should serve. Its experiments match $\gamma$ to each dataset's expected minimum query selectivity: $\gamma = 12$ for SIFT1M and Paper (12 equally likely labels, $s = 0.083$), $\gamma = 30$ for LAION, and $\gamma = 80$ for TripClick. **Paper** is about 2 million 200-dimensional embeddings of passages from a corpus of academic papers, labeled like SIFT1M. **TripClick** is about 1.06 million 768-dimensional embeddings of health-search passages, filtered by lists of clinical areas and by publication-date ranges, so its predicates are far more varied. Build time and memory grow with $\gamma$, so you do not want it larger than needed.

**Falling back.** Below $s_{\min}$ the predicate subgraph may disconnect even in ACORN, but those are exactly the queries where pre-filtering is cheap: its cost $sn$ is small. So ACORN uses a cost-based rule: if the estimated selectivity is above $1/\gamma$, search the ACORN index; otherwise pre-filter and brute-force. The paper also suggests a diagnostic: compare hybrid recall with plain HNSW ANN recall at the same $M$ and efc (ef construction, the beam width used while building the graph), and if hybrid recall is much worse, increase $\gamma$ from its starting value of $1/s_{\min}$.

**Where the estimate comes from.** The paper assumes a selectivity estimate is available and does not say how to get one. Engines use their filter indexes, as the planners in the previous course showed: Weaviate builds the allow list and Lucene evaluates the filter per segment, so both know the match count before the graph search, while Qdrant estimates cardinality from payload indexes. For an AND of conditions, [Qdrant's estimator](https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/blob/master/lib/segment/src/index/query_estimator.rs) multiplies the per-condition fractions, which assumes independence.

Correlated conditions break that. `city = Paris` (s = 0.05) AND `country = France` (s = 0.06) is estimated at 0.05 x 0.06 = 0.003, yet every Paris record is in France, so the true s is 0.05, about 17x higher. With $\gamma = 50$ (cutoff 0.02) the query is pre-filtered when the graph would have served it: slower, still exact. An anti-correlated pair errs the other way and sends a nearly empty filter into the graph.

scenes.caption: ACORN is configured with a minimum selectivity s_min = 1/gamma. Each query's predicate selectivity is estimated before search.

Example: SIFT1M with gamma = 12, predicate 'label in {1, 2, 3}' passes 3 in 12 records. s = 0.25 is above 1/gamma = 0.083, the expected filtered degree 384 x 0.25 = 96 exceeds M, so the graph is searched.

TripClick's 1st-percentile predicate has s = 0.0127, just above 1/80 = 0.0125 with gamma = 80. Anything below would be pre-filtered: 0.0125 x 1.06M vectors is about 13,200 distances, with perfect recall.
Estimation errors cut both ways: wrongly pre-filtering keeps perfect recall at lower QPS; wrongly searching ACORN gives up the perfect recall pre-filtering would have delivered at similar QPS.

blocks.prompt: Pre-filtering on SIFT1M at s = 1/12 always scans every passing vector. How many distance computations is that, and how does it compare with ACORN-gamma's 611 in Table 3?
blocks.reveal: $sn = 10^6 / 12 \approx 83{,}333$ distance computations, about **136x** ACORN-$\gamma$'s 611 (and it gives perfect recall). Pre-filtering's cost is linear in $sn$, so it only wins when $sn$ is small, which is why the fallback threshold is a selectivity, not a fixed count.

scenes.caption: From the paper's Table 3 (s = 1/12). ACORN-gamma needs 53.5% more than an HNSW built only on the passing points, ACORN-1 151% more, post-filtering 363% more.

blocks.md:
**Reported results** (Recall@10 vs QPS, ACORN, pre- and post-filtering implemented in FAISS-based C++, other baselines from their released code, all on one machine):

- Overall 2x to 1,000x higher QPS at 0.9 recall than prior methods.
- SIFT1M and Paper (12 equality labels): 2x to 10x over Filtered-DiskANN and NHQ.
- TripClick and LAION-1M (date ranges, keyword lists, regex): 30x to 50x over pre- and post-filtering, which the specialized indices cannot run.
- LAION-25M: over three orders of magnitude more QPS than the next baseline.
- Across TripClick selectivity percentiles, 5x to 50x at 0.9 recall, with pre-filtering most competitive at the 1st percentile ($s = 0.0127$).

**How the alternatives differ.** *Filtered-DiskANN* (Gollapudi et al., WWW 2023) builds label-aware Vamana graphs: FilteredVamana prunes with a filter-aware rule and uses a start node per label; StitchedVamana builds one graph per label and overlays them. It handles about 1,000 labels with equality filters. *NHQ* (Wang et al., 2022) builds a composite index and joint pruning over vectors and attributes, and the ACORN paper notes it supports only equality predicates with one attribute per record. ACORN instead never sees predicates at build time, which is why it can serve regex and range filters.

**In production: Weaviate.** Weaviate's engineering blog describes an ACORN filter strategy based on ACORN-1. It keeps vanilla HNSW indexing (so existing data needs no re-index), uses two-hop expansion **only when the connecting node fails the filter**, and randomly seeds extra entry points that match the filter. It is one value of the `filterStrategy` index setting; the docs now list `acorn` as the default, beside the older `sweeping` and a newer `pathseer`. Very restrictive filters still switch to flat brute-force search (the flat-search cutoff). In their tests ACORN helped most when filters and queries had low correlation (up to about 10x), while sweeping won at high correlation and at 50% selectivity. The last lesson compares this with Lucene, Elasticsearch and Qdrant.

ACORN is not free accuracy. The paper gives no connectivity guarantee for arbitrary data (neither does HNSW); connectivity is shown empirically. Very selective or strongly clustered predicates still need the pre-filter fallback, and ACORN-$\gamma$'s build is far slower than HNSW (SIFT1M 148.9 s vs 11.3 s, LAION-25M 38,007.5 s vs 1,147.2 s).

blocks.question: Your workload's predicates range from s = 0.002 to 0.6 over 50M vectors. You build ACORN-gamma with M = 32. What is a sensible plan?
options: gamma = 500 so every query uses the graph
gamma = 1/s_min for a moderate s_min such as 0.02 (gamma = 50), and pre-filter anything estimated below 0.02
gamma = 1 and rely on post-filtering for low selectivity
Skip ACORN: pre-filter everything because it is exact
blocks.explain: Pre-filtering at s = 0.02 over 50M is about 1M distances, costly but bounded; going lower makes it cheaper still. gamma = 500 would multiply build time and upper-level memory enormously. Post-filtering is weakest at low selectivity. Pre-filtering everything costs up to 30M distances per query at s = 0.6.

blocks.question: The selectivity estimator says s = 0.05 but the true value is 0.005, below 1/gamma = 0.02. ACORN searches the graph. What is the most likely consequence?
options: Lower recall, because the predicate subgraph may be disconnected where pre-filtering would have been fast and exact
Higher latency but perfect recall
A wrong-type error, since the predicate is not indexed
No effect, because ACORN truncates to M
blocks.explain: At s = 0.005 the expected filtered degree gamma x M x s = 50 x 32 x 0.005 = 8 is far below M, so search may get stuck. The paper notes this direction of error trades away the exactness pre-filtering would have given. The opposite error (pre-filtering when s was high) costs only speed.

lessons.title: ACORN in production engines, and where it stops helping

blocks.md:
Three widely used engines ship an ACORN mode, and all three chose **ACORN-1 on their existing, pruned HNSW graph** rather than ACORN-$\gamma$. The reasons follow from earlier lessons: ACORN-$\gamma$ builds 9x to 53x slower than ACORN-1 in the paper, stores up to $M\gamma$ links per node on upper levels, and fixes $s_{\min}$ at build time. ACORN-1 needs no rebuild, so it can be switched on for data that is already indexed. The lab's ACORN-1 on the pruned graph showed it costs little recall at moderate selectivity.

Each engine then adapts the lookup, because always expanding every neighbor wastes predicate checks where most neighbors already pass.

**Weaviate** (the `acorn` filter strategy, the default in current versions) keeps vanilla HNSW indexing and differs from the paper in three ways its blog lists:

1. No change to construction, to limit the overhead of unpruned lists; the team found the recall impact acceptable.
2. Two-hop expansion only when the connecting node fails the filter. In regions where most nodes pass, the walk behaves like ordinary HNSW.
3. Extra entry points that match the filter are seeded at random on level 0, which helps when the filter has low correlation with the query.

The flat-search cutoff (`flatSearchCutoff`) still applies first. The blog reports up to 10x over `sweeping` for low-correlation filters, while `sweeping` stays faster at high correlation.

**Lucene** (since 10.2) and **Elasticsearch** (since 9.1) use a variation of ACORN-1 by default for filtered kNN. Lucene's [FilteredHnswGraphSearcher](https://github.com/apache/lucene/blob/main/lucene/core/src/java/org/apache/lucene/util/hnsw/FilteredHnswGraphSearcher.java) scores only accepted nodes and adds these heuristics:

- It is used only when fewer than 60% of a segment's vectors pass (the default threshold in `KnnSearchStrategy`); Elastic's tests found the gains level off near 60%.
- It reads neighbors' lists only when more than 10% of the immediate neighbors are filtered out.
- It stops collecting once it has about $n_{\text{nbr}} / (1 - f)$ nodes to score, where $f$ is the filtered fraction of the $n_{\text{nbr}}$ neighbors, capped by a multiplier.
- For very restrictive filters it may branch past the second hop, within a bound.

The per-segment exact fallback from the previous course still applies. Elastic reports typical speedups of 5x.

blocks.title: Lucene's decision at one visited node (simplified)

scenes.caption: Filter passes 5% of the segment, max_conn = 32 for illustration. The multiplier is round(min(20, 16)) = 16.
Sparse spot: 2 of 32 neighbors pass. filtered = 0.9375, so the target is 32 x min(16, 16) = 512 nodes to score, and the second hop runs because 0.9375 > 0.10.
Middle: 24 of 32 pass. filtered = 0.25, target int(32 x 1.333) = 42. The second hop runs only until 42 passing nodes are collected, then stops.
Dense spot: 30 of 32 pass. filtered = 0.0625 is under the 0.10 threshold, so no list is expanded: the node is handled like plain HNSW.
scenes.output: 30 nodes to score, no second hop

blocks.md:
**Qdrant** documents ACORN as an extension of its regular HNSW search based on ACORN-1: during traversal it explores neighbors of neighbors when direct neighbors are filtered out. It is off by default and enabled per query (`params.acorn.enable`); it then applies only when the estimated selectivity is below `max_selectivity` (default 0.4). The docs call it significantly slower, about 2 to 10x in typical cases, but better in recall for restrictive filters.

Qdrant needs it less often because its filterable HNSW adds extra edges per indexed payload field. The docs name the cases those edges miss: a combination of several strict filters, since edges are built per index and not per combination, and a graph with many soft-deleted points.

blocks.title: How a filtered query is routed: paper and engines

scenes.caption: The paper: one estimate, one threshold. Below 1/gamma, pre-filter; otherwise search ACORN-gamma, whose stored lists replace the two-hop walk. There is no plain HNSW path.

Weaviate builds the allow list, so it knows the count. Below flatSearchCutoff it scans the matches. Otherwise filterStrategy picks the walk: acorn (the default), sweeping (traverse-through) or pathseer.

Lucene and Elasticsearch decide per segment. Few matches: score them exactly. Under 60% passing: the ACORN-1 style searcher. Otherwise the plain filtered walk. A walk that exceeds its visit budget also falls back to the exact scan.

Qdrant estimates cardinality from payload indexes. Small: read matches from the payload index and score them. ACORN is opt-in per query and runs below max_selectivity (default 0.4); otherwise the filterable HNSW with its payload edges.
The shared shape: count first, scan small match sets exactly, keep the standard HNSW graph for the rest, and add two-hop expansion only where filtering thins the neighborhood.

blocks.md: The production recipe is the same everywhere: keep the standard HNSW graph, expand to two hops only where filtering has thinned the neighborhood, and keep an exact scan for small match sets. The paper supplies the idea; the engines supply the conditions that decide when to use it.

**Where ACORN stops helping.**

- *Broad filters.* When most nodes pass, few neighbors fail and plain filtered HNSW is already efficient. Lucene switches its ACORN-style search off at 60% passing, and Qdrant by default at 40% (`max_selectivity` 0.4).
- *Strong negative correlation.* ACORN avoids the $O(n)$ walk, but the walk to a distant region still costs: 3,538 distances for 0.983 recall in the lab. Weaviate's seeded entry points target this case, and its docs say ACORN still beats the newer PathSeer strategy for sparse, negatively correlated filters.
- *Clustered predicates* break the independence assumption behind $\gamma = 1/s_{\min}$ (lesson 5's lab).

- *Inserts and deletes.* The paper builds by inserting points like HNSW, so inserts work, but each costs more: construction is $O(n\gamma\log n\log\gamma)$. The paper does not evaluate deletes. Engines treat deleted documents as one more filter (Elastic says so directly). If a deleted node stays in the graph as a failing node, a two-hop lookup can still pass through its list; if it were unlinked, the nodes that compression pruned in favor of it would lose that route.
- *Range predicates* are not a limit: ACORN never looks at predicates at build time, and the paper's TripClick workload filters by date ranges. Specialized indexes such as Filtered-DiskANN cannot serve them.

**Benchmarks.** The NeurIPS'23 Big-ANN competition ran a filtered track: 10 million Flickr images from the YFCC100M collection as 192-dimensional CLIP embeddings, each with a bag of tags from a 200,386-word vocabulary, and 100,000 queries with one or two tags that must all match. Entries were ranked by queries per second at 90% recall@10 on an 8-vCPU machine. The winner, ParlayANN, reached 37,902 QPS on the public queries, more than 11x the Faiss baseline, with indexes keyed by tag: a graph and an inverted index for common tags, linear scans for rare ones, and intersections for two-tag queries.

That is the label-specialized approach ACORN argues against needing. On a fixed vocabulary of equality filters it wins; ACORN's case is generality, for predicates you cannot enumerate in advance.

blocks.question: An Elasticsearch filtered kNN query is slow, and its filter passes 60% of the documents. Will Lucene's ACORN-1 style search help?
options: Yes: ACORN beats plain filtered HNSW for every filter, so it runs on every filtered query
Yes, once gamma is raised to 1/0.6 in the index mapping
No: Lucene uses it only below 60% passing, where it pays off; at 60% few neighbors fail, so look for the slowness elsewhere
No, because Elasticsearch applies kNN filters only after the search
blocks.explain: Lucene's default threshold is 60: the ACORN-style searcher runs only when fewer than 60% of the segment's vectors pass, and Elastic's tests found the gains level off near 60%. At s = 0.6 the plain walk wastes little on failing nodes. Elasticsearch has no gamma, and kNN filters run during the search.

blocks.question: A Qdrant collection has payload indexes on brand and color. Each value is common, but the query brand = X AND color = Y matches few points, and recall is poor. Which fix follows the docs?
options: Enable ACORN for the query; it applies when the estimated selectivity is below max_selectivity
Nothing: the extra HNSW edges cover every combination of indexed fields
Rebuild the collection with gamma = 1/s_min
Drop the payload indexes so the graph has no extra edges
blocks.explain: Qdrant builds extra edges per payload index, not per combination, so a combination of strict filters can still disconnect the graph; that is the case its docs name for ACORN. It is about 2 to 10x slower, hence the max_selectivity threshold (default 0.4). Qdrant has no gamma, and dropping indexes also loses the cardinality estimates.

blocks.question: Why did Weaviate, Lucene and Qdrant all ship ACORN-1 variants rather than ACORN-gamma?
options: ACORN-gamma reached lower recall than ACORN-1 in the paper
ACORN-gamma must know the predicates at build time
ACORN-1 removes the need for an exact fallback on restrictive filters
ACORN-1 runs on the HNSW graph already built: no gamma-times-larger lists and no rebuild, for more lookups per visited node
blocks.explain: ACORN-gamma is faster at search in the paper but builds 9x to 53x slower and stores longer lists; ACORN-1 works on existing graphs, which Weaviate cites directly (no reindexing). Both variants are predicate-agnostic, and every engine still keeps an exact scan for small match sets.
